newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat rebounds to strong close on EU news.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat rebounds to strong close on EU news.

text.p: CBOT wheat futures closed strongly higher Thursday as the European Commission closed its weekly export tender for 1996-97 soft wheat, traders said.

"The EU action is really the catalyst for this," said Charlie Sernatinger, grain analyst for E.D. and F. Man International. "It exacerbates an already tight supply situation worldwide. Basically, it is just us and Canada as the sole remaining sellers in the world until October."
Dry weather in European wheat areas, especially in France, was cited as a key factor in the closure of the weekly export tenders by the European Commission.
Also European grain officials said the timing of a new export tender for 1997-98 (July/June) depends on the weather.
CBOT traders said futures also were boosted by reports indicating the EU would place an export tax on wheat exports to further slow the exodus of wheat from the EU.
"The talk is, they have slapped on an export tax to stop wheat from leaving (being exported) due to the drought in France and Spain," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.
Wheat closed seven to 18-1/2 cents per bushel higher, with May up 18-1/2 at $4.25-1/4 a bushel. New crop July closed 15-1/2 cents higher at $4.31.

Wheat futures also found support on USDA's weekly export sales report. USDA Thursday said U.S. net export sales of wheat for the 1996-97 marketing year totaled 263,900 tonnes during the week ended April 10. That tally was above the range of expectations for 100,000 to 200,000 tonnes.
Weather in the U.S. received mixed reviews.
"I think a lot of people who planned to raise their forecast for the wheat crop just left it unchanged after the freeze," a trader said.

Freezing temperatures over the weekend in portions of the U.S. Great Plains triggered talk that up to 200 million bushels of wheat may have been lost. But a widely-followed analytical firm pegged the losses at roughly 50 million bushels, traders said.
Lows in the U.S. Central Plains overnight Wednesday were not cold enough to damage winter wheat, but freezing weather was expected in the eastern Corn Belt Thursday night, a U.S. meteorologist said.

The wheat futures markets, especially the Minneapolis Grain Exchange spring wheat market, remained on edge, pending prospective seeding delays for the U.S. spring wheat crop. Wet weather, including flooding, in the Northern U.S. Midwest continues to stall spring wheat fieldwork and seedings.
Canada and the U.S. were at odds Thursday concerning Canadian shipments of wheat into the U.S.
A senior USDA official said Thursday it was "our understanding" that Canada had agreed to limit its wheat and barley exports to the U.S. this year to no more than 1.5 million tonnes.
But Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale denied Canada was planning to limit grain exports to the U.S.
Merrill Lynch Futures bought five million bushels of July and ABN-Chicago Corp sold two million July and bought one million bushels of July, traders said.
Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 33,000 contracts, above the 25,959 traded Wednesday.

In wheat options, Cargill Investor Services bought 600 July $4.50 calls at 14-1/2 cents, Smith Barney bought 300 July $3.80 puts at 6-1/2 cents and Goldenberg Hehmeyer bought 600 July $4.50 calls at 14-1/2 cents and sold 600 May $4.20 calls at 1-1/2 cents, traders said.
Wheat options volume was estimated at 15,000 contracts, above the 11,492 traded Wednesday.
